extracted.intended_audience: graphic designers and creative professionals, especially book cover designers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and attitudes for designing book covers, distilled from Chip Kidd's quotes and practice — covering process, formal considerations, scale, longevity, and the cover's role relative to the book. Useful for designers creating covers for print and digital contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visually solving a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: "And that is what it always amounts to: visually solving a problem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kidd's process: read the book, brood, then respond. The designer's task is to diagnose what the book 'needs' visually and produce a solution; this may involve photographers, illustrators or other resources. The emphasis is on problem-solving rather than decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work effectively at thumbnail / small scale
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the lessons I learned in school is that the whole point of a thumbnail drawing, a tiny little sketch, is that if something looks good small, if it’s effective small, it’s going to look great when it’s bigger."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs must be legible and conceptually clear at very small sizes (postage-stamp thumbnails on screens). If the idea reads in thumbnail, it will scale up; if it fails small, it will fail in many real contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover is not the sole determinant of sales
rubrics_metrics.description: "Jurassic Park would absolutely have sold a similar amount, whether it had my cover on or not. I’m very much against the idea that the cover will sell the book... the cover is only a small part of that."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overclaiming the cover's commercial power. The cover should connect honestly with the book and its audience, but recognize marketing, author, and content are central to sales. Don't design purely as a 'sales gimmick' divorced from the book's essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite words and pictures so they mean something together
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you’re writing you’re basically designing with words... With design, you’re taking a combination of words and pictures and putting them together so that they will mean something when they’re united."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typography, imagery, and layout must be composed to produce a single coherent message. Consider the relationship between title/author text and visual elements as a unit — not separate parts — to convey meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for longevity / archival sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "I try to imagine what X will look like in five years. What will it look like in 10 years? What will it look like in 20 years?... Will this look good a long time from now or will it look dated?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for hardcover/archival editions, aim for designs that age well. Consider whether trends will date the design and whether the cover will remain appropriate and attractive over years or decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal contrasts and basic formal considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: "And there are certain basic formal considerations that won’t change. Big and small, dark and light, certain conceptual things; that’s kind of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to scale relationships, value contrast (dark/light), and clear conceptual framing. These formal principles are enduring tools for achieving clarity and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace limits as creative possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a lot of ways book cover design is really quite limited. Which is good. There’s a saying one of my teachers used to have, which is that limits are possibilities and, if your choices are limited, you’re forced to think more."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat constraints (size, production, client requirements) as productive. Restrictions can focus creative thinking and lead to stronger, more disciplined solutions rather than being obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure multi-context functionality (thumbnail, shelf, table, devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Book covers are important because books, regardless of their form, need a face. They need some kind of visual representation, whether you’re going to be seeing them the size of a postage stamp on a computer screen or a smartphone, or sitting on a table, or on a shelf, or in a bookstore."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must succeed across contexts: digital thumbnails, mobile displays, bookstore shelves, tables, and physical handling. Test legibility, composition, and recognition in each relevant context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough engagement with text and a concept-first process
rubrics_metrics.description: "I read the book, I brood, then eventually respond."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before designing, deeply engage with the manuscript. Let concepts emerge from reading and reflection rather than defaulting to surface or clichéd solutions. Concept-first workflow produces more meaningful covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize communication and function over personal artistic style
rubrics_metrics.description: "I see myself as a graphic designer, not an artist. I think that I get recognition for my work only because it’s standard that your name gets put on the back flap of the book if you’re a book designer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View the role as communicating the book to readers rather than self-expression. While a designer's sensibility matters, the priority is clarity, appropriateness, and serving the book and publisher, not showcasing the designer's ego.
